Pull request #21389: ENH: `scipy.stats`: add normal-inverse-gamma distribution

#### Reference issue
Closes gh-6528, gh-13644 (duplicate)
Supersedes gh-6739, gh-18109
https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-dev/2020-May/024185.html

#### What does this implement/fix?
This implements the normal-inverse-gamma distribution. (The multivariate generalization can be a separate PR, probably implemented in an unrelated class. I don't see any impediments to following a similar interface.)

There were two earlier PRs for this distribution:
- gh-6739 was closed because it became inactive. It was also not vectorized, and there may have been some license-related concerns.
- gh-18109 was closed because it did not implement the (bivariate) normal-inverse-gamma distribution. 

This PR addresses these concerns: it implements the normal-inverse-gamma distribution with arguments $x$ and $\sigma^2$ and shapes $\mu$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$, all of which can be broadcastable arrays.

#### Additional information
To addressed the points from the [closing comment](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/18109#issuecomment-1458993415) of gh-18109:

> It looks like the distribution is an oddball - it doesn't fit our univariate distribution infrastructure or the multivariate distribution infrastructure. 

There is essentially no multivariate distribution infrastructure, so I don't see any conflicts with it. This is the first of the multivariate distributions that is not arbitrary-dimensional, but that does not really present any complications. The more unusual thing is that the two dimensions - $x$ and $\sigma^2$ - are conceptually distinct. For instance, in the generalized version of this distribution, the normal-inverse-Wishart, $x$ becomes a vector and $\sigma^2$ becomes a matrix. As discussed in [Adding Normal-Inverse Wishart Distribution in scipy.stats module](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-dev/2020-May/024185.html), the question becomes whether we want to treat $x$ and $\sigma^2$ as separate inputs/outputs of `pdf`/`rvs` or whether we want to combine them. I've kept them separate, and normal broadcasting rules apply.

> Julia's [`ConjugatePriors.jl`](https://github.com/JuliaStats/ConjugatePriors.jl) package considers both `x` and `sig2` as random variates while R's [`PIGShift`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PIGShift/PIGShift.pdf) package considers only `x` as the random variate. Should SciPy follow the former or the latter convention?

The issues have requested the normal-inverse-gamma distribution, which is a bivariate distribution, so this PR follows the former convention. We could add methods that return related univariate distributions (e.g. for the marginal distributions).

> Would the implementation of the distribution be useful? The marginal distributions for `x` and `sig2` are already implemented in SciPy and it's easy to compute the full distribution using those.

It is relatively straightforward to generate random variates using `invgamma` and `norm`, but:
- users have requested this distribution anyway, and
- this distribution has other methods.

> The CDF on Wikipedia seems incorrect. Probably best to avoid implementing it before confirming the closed form is correct.

This PR does not implement the CDF. Not many of our multivariate distributions do, so that should be fine for an initial PR.

+    q_ancillas = q[num_ctrl_qubits + 1 :]

+

+        qc.rccx(q_controls[j], q_ancillas[i - 1], q_ancillas[i])

+    CCX gates.

+    Args:
+        num_ladder_qubits: No. of qubits involved in the ladder operation.
+
+    Returns:
+        A tuple consisting of the linear-depth ladder circuit and the index of control qubit to
+        apply the final CCX gate.
+
+    Raises:
+        QiskitError: If num_ladder_qubits <= 2.
+
+    References:
+        1. Khattar and Gidney, Rise of conditionally clean ancillae for optimizing quantum circuits
+        `arXiv:2407.17966 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17966>`__
+    """

+    if num_ladder_qubits <= 2:
+        raise QiskitError("n_ctrls >= 3 to use MCX ladder. Otherwise, use CCX")
+
+    n = num_ladder_qubits + 1

+    # down-ladder

+
+    Args:
+        num_ctrl_qubits: The number of control qubits.
+
+    Returns:
+        The synthesized quantum circuit.

+def _n_parallel_ccx_x(n: int) -> QuantumCircuit:
+    r"""
+    Construct a quantum circuit for creating n-condionally clean ancillae using 3n qubits. This
+    implements Fig. 4a of [1]. The order of returned qubits is qr_a, qr_a, qr_target.
+
+    Args:
+        n: Number of conditionally clean ancillae to create.
+
+    Returns:
+        QuantumCircuit: The quantum circuit for creating n-condionally clean ancillae.
+
+    References:
+        1. Khattar and Gidney, Rise of conditionally clean ancillae for optimizing quantum circuits
+        `arXiv:2407.17966 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17966>`__
+    """
+
+    n_qubits = 3 * n
+    q = QuantumRegister(n_qubits, name="q")
+    qc = QuantumCircuit(q, name=f"ccxn_{n}")
+    qr_a, qr_b, qr_target = q[:n], q[n : 2 * n], q[2 * n :]
+    qc.x(qr_target)
+    qc.ccx(qr_a, qr_b, qr_target)
+
+    return qc
+
+
+def _build_logn_depth_ccx_ladder(
+    ancilla_idx: int, ctrls: list[int], skip_cond_clean: bool = False
+) -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, list[int]]:
+    r"""
+    Helper function to build a log-depth ladder compose of CCX and X gates as shown in Fig. 4b of [1].
+
+    Args:
+        ancilla_idx: Index of the ancillary qubit.
+        ctrls: List of control qubits.
+        skip_cond_clean: If True, do not include the conditionally clean ancilla (step 1 and 5 in
+            Fig. 4b of [1]).
+
+    Returns:
+        A tuple consisting of the log-depth ladder circuit of conditionally clean ancillae and the
+        list of indices of control qubit to apply the linear-depth MCX gate.
+
+    Raises:
+        QiskitError: If no. of qubits in parallel CCX + X gates are not the same.
+
+    References:
+        1. Khattar and Gidney, Rise of conditionally clean ancillae for optimizing quantum circuits
+        `arXiv:2407.17966 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17966>`__
+    """
+
+    qc = QuantumCircuit(len(ctrls) + 1)
+    anc = [ancilla_idx]
+    final_ctrls = []
+
+    while len(ctrls) > 1:
+        next_batch_len = min(len(anc) + 1, len(ctrls))
+        ctrls, nxt_batch = ctrls[next_batch_len:], ctrls[:next_batch_len]
+        new_anc = []
+        while len(nxt_batch) > 1:
+            ccx_n = len(nxt_batch) // 2
+            st = int(len(nxt_batch) % 2)
+            ccx_x, ccx_y, ccx_t = (
+                nxt_batch[st : st + ccx_n],
+                nxt_batch[st + ccx_n :],
+                anc[-ccx_n:],
+            )
+            if not len(ccx_x) == len(ccx_y) == ccx_n >= 1:
+                raise QiskitError(
+                    f"Invalid CCX gate parameters: {len(ccx_x)=} != {len(ccx_y)=} != {len(ccx_n)=}"
+                )
+            if ccx_t != [ancilla_idx]:
+                qc.compose(_n_parallel_ccx_x(ccx_n), ccx_x + ccx_y + ccx_t, inplace=True)
+            else:
+                if not skip_cond_clean:
+                    qc.ccx(ccx_x[0], ccx_y[0], ccx_t[0])  #  # create conditionally clean ancilla
+            new_anc += nxt_batch[st:]  #                     # newly created cond. clean ancilla
+            nxt_batch = ccx_t + nxt_batch[:st]
+            anc = anc[:-ccx_n]
+
+        anc = sorted(anc + new_anc)
+        final_ctrls += nxt_batch
+
+    final_ctrls += ctrls
+    final_ctrls = sorted(final_ctrls)
+    return qc, final_ctrls[:-1]  # exclude ancilla
+

+def synth_mcx_2_kg24(num_ctrl_qubits: int, clean: bool = True) -> QuantumCircuit:
+    r"""
+    Synthesize a multi-controlled X gate with :math:`k` controls using :math:`2` ancillary qubits.
+    as described in Sec. 5 of [1].
+
+    Args:
+        num_ctrl_qubits: The number of control qubits.
+        clean: If True, the ancilla is clean, otherwise it is dirty.
+
+    Returns:
+        The synthesized quantum circuit.
+
+    Raises:
+        QiskitError: If num_ctrl_qubits <= 2.
+
+    References:
+        1. Khattar and Gidney, Rise of conditionally clean ancillae for optimizing quantum circuits
+        `arXiv:2407.17966 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.17966>`__
+    """
+
+    if num_ctrl_qubits <= 2:
+        raise QiskitError("kg24 synthesis requires at least 3 control qubits. Use CCX directly.")
+
+    q_control = QuantumRegister(num_ctrl_qubits, name="ctrl")
+    q_target = QuantumRegister(1, name="targ")
+    q_ancilla = AncillaRegister(2, name="anc")
+    qc = QuantumCircuit(q_control, q_target, q_ancilla, name="mcx_logn_depth")
+
+    ladder_ops, final_ctrls = _build_logn_depth_ccx_ladder(
+        num_ctrl_qubits, list(range(num_ctrl_qubits))
+    )
+    qc.compose(ladder_ops, q_control[:] + [q_ancilla[0]], inplace=True)
+    if len(final_ctrls) == 1:  # Already a toffoli
+        qc.ccx(q_ancilla[0], q_control[final_ctrls[0]], q_target)
+    else:
+        mid_mcx = synth_mcx_1_clean_kg24(len(final_ctrls) + 1)
+        qc.compose(
+            mid_mcx,
+            [q_ancilla[0]]
+            + q_control[final_ctrls]
+            + q_target[:]
+            + [q_ancilla[1]],  # ctrls, targ, anc
+            inplace=True,
+        )
+    qc.compose(ladder_ops.inverse(), q_control[:] + [q_ancilla[0]], inplace=True)
+
+    if not clean:
+        # perform toggle-detection if ancilla is dirty
+        ladder_ops_new, final_ctrls = _build_logn_depth_ccx_ladder(
+            num_ctrl_qubits, list(range(num_ctrl_qubits)), skip_cond_clean=True
+        )
+        qc.compose(ladder_ops_new, q_control[:] + [q_ancilla[0]], inplace=True)
+        if len(final_ctrls) == 1:
+            qc.ccx(q_ancilla[0], q_control[final_ctrls[0]], q_target)
+        else:
+            qc.compose(
+                mid_mcx,
+                [q_ancilla[0]] + q_control[final_ctrls] + q_target[:] + [q_ancilla[1]],
+                inplace=True,
+            )
+        qc.compose(ladder_ops_new.inverse(), q_control[:] + [q_ancilla[0]], inplace=True)
+
+    return qc
+
+
+def synth_mcx_2_clean_kg24(num_ctrl_qubits: int) -> QuantumCircuit:

Pull request #12814: Light Cone Transpiler Pass

### Summary
When measuring or sampling a subset of the qubits of our circuit there will be some gates in our circuit that will not affect the outcome of the measurement. This transpiler pass provides an easy tool to reduce the number of gates in our circuit provided a Pauli observable to be measured or  a subset of measurements in the Z basis.

What this pull request is about:

---
Pull request #14024: Introduce custom sympy srepr parser

### Summary

This commit introduces a custom parser to QPY for parameter expression payloads that were generated using sympy. Prior to QPY version 10 this was the only way we supported serializing parameter expressions in QPY. For QPY version 10, 11, and 12 sympy could optionally be used if the payload was generated explicitly to not use symengine (in qiskit 1.0 it defaulted to use symengine).

This serialization format relied on sympy to generate a string representation of the expression which we then put in the payload. On deserialization we called sympy's parse_expr() function which internally is calling sympy's sympify() internally. Sympy documents that sympify() relies on Python's eval() for string input and should not be used with untrusted input. But parse_expr() didn't have such a warning (at the time, I plan to contribute adding one), so using this function provides an avenue for arbitrary code execution during QPY deserialization.

This commit fixes this issue by writing a custom parser for the string representation in a QPY payload based on python's ast module. This parser walks the abstract syntax tree and builds the sympy expression object as it it goes. It is restricted to the operations that ParameterExpression supports and if any part of the string tries to use functionality outside that set it will error.

+    "tan",
+    "atan",
+    "acos",
+    "asin",
+    "exp",
+    "conjugate",
+}

+UNARY = {
+    "sin",
+    "cos",
+    "tan",
+    "atan",
+    "acos",
+    "asin",
+    "conjugate",
+    "Symbol",
+    "Integer",
+    "Complex",
+    "Abs",
+    "Float",
+}

+class ParseSympyWalker(ast.NodeVisitor):
+    """A custom ast walker that is passed the sympy srepr from QPY < 13 and creates a custom
+    expression."""
+
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.stack = []
+
+    def visit_UnaryOp(self, node: ast.UnaryOp):  # pylint: disable=invalid-name
+        """Visit a python unary op node"""
+        self.visit(node.operand)
+        arg = self.stack.pop()
+        if isinstance(node.op, ast.UAdd):
+            self.stack.append(+arg)
+        elif isinstance(node.op, ast.USub):
+            self.stack.append(-arg)
+        elif isinstance(node.op, ast.Not):
+            self.stack.append(not arg)
+        elif isinstance(node.op, ast.Invert):
+            self.stack.append(~arg)
+        else:
+            raise QpyError(f"Invalid unary op as part of sympy srepr: {node.op}")
+
+    def visit_Constant(self, node: ast.Constant):  # pylint: disable=invalid-name
+        """Visit a constant node."""
+        self.stack.append(node.value)
+
+    def visit_Call(self, node: ast.Call):  # pylint: disable=invalid-name
+        """Visit a call node
+
+        This can only be parameter expression allowed sympy call types.
+        """
+        import sympy
+
+        if isinstance(node.func, ast.Name):
+            name = node.func.id
+        else:
+            raise QpyError("Unknown node type")
+
+        if name not in ALLOWED_CALLERS:
+            raise QpyError(f"{name} is not part of a valid sympy expression srepr")
+
+        args = node.args
+        if name in UNARY:
+            if len(args) != 1:
+                raise QpyError(f"{name} has an invalid number of args in sympy srepr")
+            self.visit(args[0])
+            obj = getattr(sympy, name)(self.stack.pop())
+            self.stack.append(obj)
+        else:
+            for arg in args:
+                self.visit(arg)
+            out_args = [self.stack.pop() for _ in range(len(args))]
+            out_args.reverse()
+            obj = getattr(sympy, name)(*out_args)
+            self.stack.append(obj)
+
+
+def parse_sympy_repr(sympy_repr: str):
+    """Parse a given sympy srepr into a symbolic expression object."""
+    tree = ast.parse(sympy_repr, mode="eval")
+    visitor = ParseSympyWalker()
+    visitor.visit(tree)
+    return visitor.stack.pop()

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

You have these tools:

- `run` — a shell, for searching and reading. `grep`, `sed`, `ls`, `cat`. Keep searches
  inside the repository; starting from `/` or `..` walks into system directories and
  will be killed. Do not run the test suite through this tool: use `run_tests`.
- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell
  redirection.
- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

Before you write, read one to three of the tests already in that directory. You are
adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they
leave alone.

Do not type a test command yourself. `run_tests` builds the right one for this project
and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

That before-and-after flip is the property your test has to have. A test that passes in
both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

- `coverage` — of the lines this pull request changed, which ones did your test actually
  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

- `mutation` — breaks the fix in small ways on purpose, runs your test against each
  broken version, and tells you which ones your test still passes on. A variant your test
  does not notice is a behaviour this change makes that your test does not check. It runs
  once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, a test that cannot tell the
  fix from no fix has nothing to say about wrong versions of it.

Use it, and act on what it says. A test can flip from failing to passing, execute every
changed line, and still be satisfied by a fix with a comparison inverted or a boundary off
by one — coverage says the line *ran*, this says whether you would have *noticed* it going
wrong. That is the difference between a test that documents the fix and a test that
merely accompanies it.

Every survivor gets an answer. Read each one as a question, not as a defect to clear:

A survivor you have not answered either way is the one thing this tool exists to prevent:
a wrong fix your test would let through without anyone having decided that is acceptable.

What you must never do is write an assertion whose purpose is to kill a mutant. Pinning
the exact expression a variant happened to change — asserting on an internal value, or

person who has to maintain it, which is the only audience that matters.

**Do not modify or delete any file that is already here.** Not the library source, not

Creating files is allowed. Your test goes in `test/python/qpy/test_f2p_Qiskit__qiskit_14024.py`, and if it genuinely needs more

Read the source before you write -- enough to know what to assert, not enough to be
certain of everything. Then get a test running, and let what it does correct the rest of

The report describes a symptom; the cause may be several layers below it and may never be

## Before you finish

Work through these checks in order. Each one answers a question the previous leaves open,
and each catches a mistake the others do not.

They are not all the same kind of thing. The first two are gates: the file runs, and the
test flips. The ones after them are instruments you work with — call one, change the test

back exactly as it found it, so you can call any of them whenever you want. When you are
done changing the test, run `verify` once more: an assertion added for any other reason
can quietly stop the test failing on the old code, and then it is no longer the test you
set out to write.

**1. `run_tests` — does the file run at all?**
 A test that errors on a typo, a missing
fixture or a name this project never had tells you nothing about the library; it never
reached the code. A name the change *adds* is different: here it does not exist yet, so an

**2. `verify` — does it flip?** Failing before the change and passing after is the
property the test exists to have, and `verify` is the only thing here that answers it.

**Call `verify`, and keep calling it until it says fail-to-pass.** That is the loop, and

looks. Each answer tells you which way to move — passes on both sides means you asserted

fails on both means the test itself is wrong rather than strict, so fix the test, not the
assertion's strength. Change the test, call `verify` again, and repeat. You are not done
with this step until it reports fail-to-pass.

**3. `coverage` — does it reach the change?** A test can flip while running only part of
what the change touched: it gets to the new code by a route that skips a branch. That test
passes today and will still pass tomorrow if that branch breaks again. The missed lines
are the inputs you did not think of, and the conditions printed above each one say what
your input has to satisfy to get there.

**Call `coverage`, and if it lists changed lines your test never runs, change the test

That is a loop, and it is checked: while `coverage` lists lines your test never runs you

each function holding a missed line gets one turn -- until none is missed or every part
has had its turn. It is not a demand that every line runs whatever it takes —
sometimes a line is genuinely outside what this test is for — it is a demand that each
missed line gets an answer rather than being noted and passed over. Decide what the missed lines are, change the test,

until what remains is missed for a reason you can state in a sentence.

Missed lines are not a bad mark. They are a description of your test, usually a precise one:
the change has more than one path through it and you took one. So ask whether the missed

What you must not do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion after it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you.

**4. `mutation` — would it notice a wrong fix?** Break the fix in small ways and see
whether your test objects. Whatever survives is a version of this change that is wrong in
a way your test cannot tell apart from the right one.

**Call it, and read what comes back.** It is the only check that asks whether your
assertions have any force, and a test that flips and covers every line can still pass
against a fix that is subtly wrong.

**Work every survivor.** For each, decide whether the behaviour it breaks is part of what
this pull request fixes. If it is, add the assertion about that behaviour and call
`verify` and `mutation` again. If it is not, leave it. This is a loop, and

closes others, and it can reveal ones the earlier version never reached.

Work through the survivors and decide about each, rather than trying to clear the list.
Where the broken behaviour is part of what the pull request fixes, add the assertion that
covers it; where it is not, say so to yourself and move on. Ending with survivors you have
considered and rejected is a good result. Ending with none because you asserted on

A check that tells you something and gets no response was not worth running. If one shows

anything else can quietly stop the test failing on the old code.

**Before you can stop, the last `verify` must say fail-to-pass, and you must not have

checked by its answer, not by whether you called it; a stop before it says fail-to-pass

**Once `verify` says fail-to-pass, the checks after it are checked by their answers, in
this order.** Each is a question about a test that already flips, so work them in
sequence:
- `coverage`, as a loop: while it lists lines your test never runs, change the test and

  break and call it again, until none survives or an honest attempt catches no more.

Calling a tool once and stopping on an answer you did nothing with does not satisfy this.
While any of these loops is open you will be sent back with the reason, so working it now
is the shorter path.

You are finished when the checks above have been run against the test as it now stands
and nothing any of them raised is still unanswered. Say in one sentence what behaviour your test pins down, and stop.

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

You have these tools:

- `run` — a shell, for searching and reading. `grep`, `sed`, `ls`, `cat`. Keep searches
  inside the repository; starting from `/` or `..` walks into system directories and
  will be killed. Do not run the test suite through this tool: use `run_tests`.
- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell
  redirection.
- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

Before you write, read one to three of the tests already in that directory. You are
adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they
leave alone.

Do not type a test command yourself. `run_tests` builds the right one for this project
and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

That before-and-after flip is the property your test has to have. A test that passes in
both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

- `coverage` — of the lines this pull request changed, which ones did your test actually
  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

- `mutation` — breaks the fix in small ways on purpose, runs your test against each
  broken version, and tells you which ones your test still passes on. A variant your test
  does not notice is a behaviour this change makes that your test does not check. It runs
  once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, a test that cannot tell the
  fix from no fix has nothing to say about wrong versions of it.

Use it, and act on what it says. A test can flip from failing to passing, execute every
changed line, and still be satisfied by a fix with a comparison inverted or a boundary off
by one — coverage says the line *ran*, this says whether you would have *noticed* it going
wrong. That is the difference between a test that documents the fix and a test that
merely accompanies it.

Every survivor gets an answer. Read each one as a question, not as a defect to clear:

- **Would a reviewer call the behaviour it breaks part of what this pull request fixes?**

  asserts it (what the code returns, raises or does for an input that tells the right fix

- **Or does the variant break something the change was never about**, or nothing
  observable at all? Then say so, in one sentence, and leave it. Not every survivor is a

A survivor you have not answered either way is the one thing this tool exists to prevent:
a wrong fix your test would let through without anyone having decided that is acceptable.

What you must never do is write an assertion whose purpose is to kill a mutant. Pinning
the exact expression a variant happened to change — asserting on an internal value, or

person who has to maintain it, which is the only audience that matters.

done changing the test, run `verify` once more: an assertion added for any other reason

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

You have these tools:

- `run` — a shell, for searching and reading. `grep`, `sed`, `ls`, `cat`. Keep searches
  inside the repository; starting from `/` or `..` walks into system directories and
  will be killed. Do not run the test suite through this tool: use `run_tests`.
- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell
  redirection.
- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

Before you write, read one to three of the tests already in that directory. You are
adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they
leave alone.

Do not type a test command yourself. `run_tests` builds the right one for this project
and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

That before-and-after flip is the property your test has to have. A test that passes in
both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

- `coverage` — of the lines this pull request changed, which ones did your test actually
  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

- `mutation` — breaks the fix in small ways on purpose, runs your test against each
  broken version, and tells you which ones your test still passes on. A variant your test
  does not notice is a behaviour this change makes that your test does not check. It runs
  once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, a test that cannot tell the
  fix from no fix has nothing to say about wrong versions of it.

Use it, and act on what it says. A test can flip from failing to passing, execute every
changed line, and still be satisfied by a fix with a comparison inverted or a boundary off
by one — coverage says the line *ran*, this says whether you would have *noticed* it going
wrong. That is the difference between a test that documents the fix and a test that
merely accompanies it.

Every survivor gets an answer. Read each one as a question, not as a defect to clear:

- **Would a reviewer call the behaviour it breaks part of what this pull request fixes?**
  If yes, your test is missing an assertion about that behaviour — add the one that
  asserts it (what the code returns, raises or does for an input that tells the right fix
  from this wrong one), and the variant dies as a consequence. Then run `verify` and
  `mutation` again.
- **Or does the variant break something the change was never about**, or nothing
  observable at all? Then say so, in one sentence, and leave it. Not every survivor is a
  gap, and a test stretched to cover one that is not gets worse, not better.

A survivor you have not answered either way is the one thing this tool exists to prevent:
a wrong fix your test would let through without anyone having decided that is acceptable.

What you must never do is write an assertion whose purpose is to kill a mutant. Pinning
the exact expression a variant happened to change — asserting on an internal value, or
restating the implementation — kills it and checks nothing a reader would recognise as
behaviour. A test like that passes every instrument here and is worthless to the next
person who has to maintain it, which is the only audience that matters.

**Do not modify or delete any file that is already here.** Not the library source, not
an existing test, not an existing fixture. The test is supposed to fail on this code —
that is the entire point — and editing what it tests destroys the measurement rather than
passing it. This is checked after every action and any such edit is reverted, so it costs
you the action and gains you nothing.

**Test what the code does, not what it says.** Do not read the project's source as text —
no `inspect.getsource`, no opening a `.py` file — and assert on its contents. Such a test

Read the source before you write -- enough to know what to assert, not enough to be
certain of everything. Then get a test running, and let what it does correct the rest of

## Before you finish

Work through these checks in order. Each one answers a question the previous leaves open,
and each catches a mistake the others do not.

They are not all the same kind of thing. The first two are gates: the file runs, and the
test flips. The ones after them are instruments you work with — call one, change the test
in the light of what it says, call it again, as many times as it takes. Nothing here is a
one-shot formality, and none of these tools costs anything but time; each puts the tree
back exactly as it found it, so you can call any of them whenever you want. When you are
done changing the test, run `verify` once more: an assertion added for any other reason
can quietly stop the test failing on the old code, and then it is no longer the test you
set out to write.

**1. `run_tests` — does the file run at all?**

fixture or a name this project never had tells you nothing about the library; it never
reached the code. A name the change *adds* is different: here it does not exist yet, so an
`ImportError`, `AttributeError` or `TypeError` about it is exactly the old behaviour, and a
test that uses it the way the change intends fails here for the right reason. Do not catch
or skip that error to make the test pass on this code. What you want to see here is the
library behaving the old way: an assertion that does not hold, the wrong exception coming
back, or a name the change adds not being there yet.

**2. `verify` — does it flip?** Failing before the change and passing after is the
property the test exists to have, and `verify` is the only thing here that answers it.

**Call `verify`, and keep calling it until it says fail-to-pass.** That is the loop, and
it is not optional: a test you have not run through `verify` is a guess, however right it
looks. Each answer tells you which way to move — passes on both sides means you asserted
something this pull request does not affect, so find what the change actually alters;
fails on both means the test itself is wrong rather than strict, so fix the test, not the
assertion's strength. Change the test, call `verify` again, and repeat. You are not done
with this step until it reports fail-to-pass.

**3. `coverage` — does it reach the change?** A test can flip while running only part of
what the change touched: it gets to the new code by a route that skips a branch. That test
passes today and will still pass tomorrow if that branch breaks again. The missed lines
are the inputs you did not think of, and the conditions printed above each one say what
your input has to satisfy to get there.

**Call `coverage`, and if it lists changed lines your test never runs, change the test
before you stop.** The aim is a test that runs every line the change touched.
That is a loop, and it is checked: while `coverage` lists lines your test never runs you
will be sent back to change the test and call it again, one part of the change at a time --
each function holding a missed line gets one turn -- until none is missed or every part
has had its turn. It is not a demand that every line runs whatever it takes —
sometimes a line is genuinely outside what this test is for — it is a demand that each
missed line gets an answer rather than being noted and passed over. Decide what the missed lines are, change the test,
call `coverage` again; you do not need to re-run the earlier checks in between. Keep going
until what remains is missed for a reason you can state in a sentence.

Missed lines are not a bad mark. They are a description of your test, usually a precise one:
the change has more than one path through it and you took one. So ask whether the missed
lines are the same behaviour reached another way -- one more assertion normally covers
that -- or a genuinely separate case the same pull request also fixed, which deserves a
second test rather than an assertion stretched to reach it.

What you must not do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion after it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you.

**4. `mutation` — would it notice a wrong fix?** Break the fix in small ways and see
whether your test objects. Whatever survives is a version of this change that is wrong in

---
Pull request #21819: ENH: `stats.ContinuousDistribution`: improve method resolution logic

#### Reference issue
Closes gh-2509

#### What does this implement/fix?
Previously, when the `tol` property of `ContinuousDistribution` was left unspecified, the CCDF/CDF could be calculated as the numerical complement of the CDF/CCDF. This logic was unusual because it ignored the *magnitude* of `tol`, and it was suboptimal because it did not protect against catastrophic cancellation in the default case (`tol` unspecified). 

This PR assesses the loss of precision when using the complement method to compute the CCDF/CDF and uses `quadrature` (in the appropriate tail) when the precision is worse than `tol`. It makes a similar adjustment to the logic of the inverse CCDF/CDF and 2-arg CDF.

There was similar logic in place for evaluating the log-CDF/CCDF as the logarithm of the CDF/CCDF. This is inaccurate when the CDF/CCDF underflows, so this PR checks for underflow and falls back to log-quadrature. It makes similar adjustments to the logic of `logexp` and 2-arg CDF.  

This PR also makes a few other small improvements/adjustments:
- The result dtype of 2-arg `logcdf` previously depended on the values of the arguments. Now, the result dtype is complex regardless of whether `y < x`.
- Fixes a copy-paste error in the `ContinuousDistribution.__sub__` method.
- Adds a private method for computing distribution moments by integrating the inverse CDF (rather than the PDF).

#### Additional information
Other obvious improvements to the default logic:

- ~~We could assess whether it is safe to compute a log-method as the logarithm of the non-log method depending on whether the non-log method over/under flows.~~ Done here.
- When the tolerance is quite strict, it might not be safe to compute a non-log method as the exponential of the log-method. We could detect this by checking `exp(logf(x)) - exp(logf(x) + np.nextafter(logf(x), np.inf)` (which is the absolute error corresponding to 1 ULP of error in `logf(x)`).
- There are also some situations in which it might be preferable to use numerical calculations rather than using log-complements or `logexpxmexpy`.
- For improvements when `locdf` and `logccdf` are not defined and the log CDF/CCDF probability is close to 0, we could apply the ideas from gh-21301 to the new infrastructure. (Note that the user can easily perform the main trick by choosing `method='complement'`; it's just not the default behavior.)

<details>
Regarding the safety of computing a non-log method as the exponential of the log-method:

```python3
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x0 = np.logspace(-300, 300, 1000)
x1 = np.log(x0)
x2 = np.nextafter(x1, np.inf)
err = abs((np.exp(x2) - np.exp(x1))/np.exp(x2))
plt.semilogy(x1, err)
plt.xlabel('`x`')
plt.ylabel('Relative Error')
plt.title('Error in `exp(x)` corresponding with 1 ULP error in `x`')
plt.show()
```

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a2167bea-8350-435c-9c0b-24c3815c5e4f)

The maximum relative error is ~1e-13. Exponentiation is only used if there is a formula for the log-method, so assuming the formula for the log-method is accurate, the exponential of the log-method will still be quite accurate.

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

Read it as evidence, not as a specification to copy. Ask what a caller can observe that
differs before and after: a different return value, an exception that is or is not
raised, a side effect that now happens. Then write the test around that observable
difference.

A change is not always one behaviour. Read every hunk, and every branch it adds or
removes, and work out what each one does for a caller: a condition that now holds, a path
that is now taken, a case that is now handled differently. Understanding the change means
being able to say what it does everywhere it acts, not only where you first recognised
it.

Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that
case. Feed such a change ordinary data and both versions agree, and the test is
indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the
answer is "the same thing", that input does not test this change and you need a
different one.

You have these tools:

- `run` — a shell, for searching and reading. `grep`, `sed`, `ls`, `cat`. Keep searches
  inside the repository; starting from `/` or `..` walks into system directories and
  will be killed. Do not run the test suite through this tool: use `run_tests`.
- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell
  redirection.
- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

Before you write, read one to three of the tests already in that directory. You are
adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they
leave alone.

Do not type a test command yourself. `run_tests` builds the right one for this project
and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

That before-and-after flip is the property your test has to have. A test that passes in
both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

- `coverage` — of the lines this pull request changed, which ones did your test actually
  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

- `mutation` — breaks the fix in small ways on purpose, runs your test against each
  broken version, and tells you which ones your test still passes on. A variant your test
  does not notice is a behaviour this change makes that your test does not check. It runs
  once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, a test that cannot tell the
  fix from no fix has nothing to say about wrong versions of it.

Use it, and act on what it says. A test can flip from failing to passing, execute every
changed line, and still be satisfied by a fix with a comparison inverted or a boundary off
by one — coverage says the line *ran*, this says whether you would have *noticed* it going
wrong. That is the difference between a test that documents the fix and a test that
merely accompanies it.

Every survivor gets an answer. Read each one as a question, not as a defect to clear:

  If yes, your test is missing an assertion about that behaviour — add the one that

- **Or does the variant break something the change was never about**, or nothing

A survivor you have not answered either way is the one thing this tool exists to prevent:
a wrong fix your test would let through without anyone having decided that is acceptable.

What you must never do is write an assertion whose purpose is to kill a mutant. Pinning

person who has to maintain it, which is the only audience that matters.

## Before you finish

Work through these checks in order. Each one answers a question the previous leaves open,
and each catches a mistake the others do not.

They are not all the same kind of thing. The first two are gates: the file runs, and the
test flips. The ones after them are instruments you work with — call one, change the test
in the light of what it says, call it again, as many times as it takes. Nothing here is a
one-shot formality, and none of these tools costs anything but time; each puts the tree
back exactly as it found it, so you can call any of them whenever you want. When you are
done changing the test, run `verify` once more: an assertion added for any other reason
can quietly stop the test failing on the old code, and then it is no longer the test you
set out to write.

**1. `run_tests` — does the file run at all?**
 A test that errors on a typo, a missing
fixture or a name this project never had tells you nothing about the library; it never
reached the code. A name the change *adds* is different: here it does not exist yet, so an
`ImportError`, `AttributeError` or `TypeError` about it is exactly the old behaviour, and a
test that uses it the way the change intends fails here for the right reason. Do not catch
or skip that error to make the test pass on this code. What you want to see here is the
library behaving the old way: an assertion that does not hold, the wrong exception coming
back, or a name the change adds not being there yet.

**2. `verify` — does it flip?** Failing before the change and passing after is the
property the test exists to have, and `verify` is the only thing here that answers it.

**Call `verify`, and keep calling it until it says fail-to-pass.** That is the loop, and
it is not optional: a test you have not run through `verify` is a guess, however right it
looks. Each answer tells you which way to move — passes on both sides means you asserted
something this pull request does not affect, so find what the change actually alters;
fails on both means the test itself is wrong rather than strict, so fix the test, not the
assertion's strength. Change the test, call `verify` again, and repeat. You are not done
with this step until it reports fail-to-pass.

**3. `coverage` — does it reach the change?** A test can flip while running only part of
what the change touched: it gets to the new code by a route that skips a branch. That test
passes today and will still pass tomorrow if that branch breaks again. The missed lines
are the inputs you did not think of, and the conditions printed above each one say what
your input has to satisfy to get there.

**Call `coverage`, and if it lists changed lines your test never runs, change the test
before you stop.** The aim is a test that runs every line the change touched.
That is a loop, and it is checked: while `coverage` lists lines your test never runs you
will be sent back to change the test and call it again, one part of the change at a time --
each function holding a missed line gets one turn -- until none is missed or every part
has had its turn. It is not a demand that every line runs whatever it takes —
sometimes a line is genuinely outside what this test is for — it is a demand that each
missed line gets an answer rather than being noted and passed over. Decide what the missed lines are, change the test,
call `coverage` again; you do not need to re-run the earlier checks in between. Keep going
until what remains is missed for a reason you can state in a sentence.

Missed lines are not a bad mark. They are a description of your test, usually a precise one:
the change has more than one path through it and you took one. So ask whether the missed
lines are the same behaviour reached another way -- one more assertion normally covers
that -- or a genuinely separate case the same pull request also fixed, which deserves a
second test rather than an assertion stretched to reach it.

What you must not do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion after it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you.

**4. `mutation` — would it notice a wrong fix?** Break the fix in small ways and see
whether your test objects. Whatever survives is a version of this change that is wrong in
a way your test cannot tell apart from the right one.

**Call it, and read what comes back.** It is the only check that asks whether your
assertions have any force, and a test that flips and covers every line can still pass
against a fix that is subtly wrong.

**Work every survivor.** For each, decide whether the behaviour it breaks is part of what
this pull request fixes. If it is, add the assertion about that behaviour and call
`verify` and `mutation` again. If it is not, leave it. This is a loop, and
it is checked: while survivors remain you will be sent back to work them and call
`mutation` again, until none survives or an honest attempt catches no more -- what is left

the list for its own sake: a run once answered `0 killed` by adding a
second test that failed on both sides, which turned a file whose first test flipped
correctly into no result at all. Keep `verify` saying fail-to-pass while you work.

Call it again after you change the test — a new assertion that closes one survivor often
closes others, and it can reveal ones the earlier version never reached.

Work through the survivors and decide about each, rather than trying to clear the list.
Where the broken behaviour is part of what the pull request fixes, add the assertion that
covers it; where it is not, say so to yourself and move on. Ending with survivors you have
considered and rejected is a good result. Ending with none because you asserted on
whatever each variant touched is not.

A check that tells you something and gets no response was not worth running. If one shows
a failure, fix the test and run it again.
If one shows lines of the change your test never reached, decide what they are -- part of
the behaviour you set out to pin down and so worth another assertion, a separate case that

behaviour is part of what the change fixes -- and if it is, assert it. If it is not, that

*Old news:*

Most of this will be pretty straightforward. There are some little things I'll want to address later (e.g. previously, `pearsonr` converted inputs to be at least `float64`, but I imagine we'd want to respect dtype with array API), but there is one big question for now:

Calculation of the p-value currently relies on the incomplete beta function, which is not among the special functions for which we have experimental array API support (gh-19023). Even if it were, calculation of the p-value currently relies on the distribution infrastructure. In any case, calculation of the statistic with an alternative array backend can easily be done now, but calculation of the p-value with an alternative array backend will take more time. 

For vectorized calculations, I think there is still value in calculating the statistic with the alternative array backend, then converting the statistic (which has been reduced by at least one dimension) to a NumPy array for calculation of the p-value. Are there objections to this?

I know there have been objections to converting non-NumPy arrays to NumPy arrays for running compiled code, but I think this is a little different, since the statistic might not even be an array after the reducing operation, and if it is, it's smaller than the original array.

Pull request #21777: ENH: stats: absolute value of a random variable

#### Reference issue
Toward gh-15928

#### What does this implement/fix?
SciPy's `foldnorm` and `foldcauchy` are examples of folded distributions, which "fold" the PDF from the left of the origin to the right. In terms of random variables, this corresponds with taking the absolute value. `halfnorm`, `halfgennorm`, `halflogistic`, and `halfcauchy` are are all special cases of folded distributions.

This PR adds a class that represents folded distributions and a function `abs` that takes the absolute value of a random variable. For example, if `X = stats.Normal()`, `Y = abs(X)` is distributed according to the folded normal. While I was at it, I went ahead and implemented the `__abs__` operator. We should probably still have our own `abs` function for the same reasons that NumPy includes `abs` in addition to overriding `__abs__` (probably documentation and discoverability). 

```python3
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

X = abs(stats.Normal() + 1.2)
X0 = stats.foldnorm(1.2)

x = np.linspace(-1, 5, 300)
pdf = X.pdf(x)
pdf0 = X0.pdf(x)
plt.plot(x, pdf, label='PDF underlying `X`')
plt.plot(x, pdf0, '--', label='PDF underlying `X0`')
plt.legend()
plt.title("PDF of a folded normal distribution")
plt.show()
```

Pull request #21996: ENH: `stats.fisher_exact`: extend to `R x C` tables

#### Reference issue
Follow-up to gh-20989, gh-15618
Closes gh-7099

#### What does this implement/fix?
This extends `fisher_exact` to two-dimensional tables with shapes other than `(2, 2)`. As the notes of `fisher_exact` already explained, there is more than one choice of statistic associated with Fisher's exact test; here, we use the PMF of [`scipy.stats.random_table`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.random_table.html) (with the marginals of the observed table) as the statistic. The p-value - the percentage of tables with the observed marginals that produce a statistic at least as extreme (small) as the observed table - is determined via either a permutation or Monte Carlo approach. Although the two approaches are exactly equivalent in this case, both may be valuable: the Monte Carlo approach is much faster because it uses `scipy.stats.random_table` to sample the tables, but the permutation approach *can* perform a deterministic exact test for sufficiently small tables. Both approaches are exact or almost exact in a long-run sense.

#### Additional information
I'll need to check the behavior for 1 x C and R x 1 tables and maybe add some edge case handling for those.
